Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, a clear and concise answer can be synthesized as follows:

To address eyelid-parotid metastasis, it is essential to thoroughly evaluate both the periocular and parotid areas. This means that oculoplastic and parotid surgeons should routinely assess these regions when patients present with a mass in either structure.

Regarding chemical shift MRI, this technique can contribute to routine dynamic contrast subtraction in morphologic analysis of solid breast masses, particularly for the evaluation of margins of benign lesions in fatty breasts. However, it is not sufficient alone for morphologic evaluation.

Cholestasis associated with small bowel atresia may be expected to resolve on its own, but it is not always necessary to investigate. A more selective approach to investigations might be warranted.

In cases of early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis, clinical identifiers have not been validated and may not be applicable. Clinicians should remain aware that commonly used identifiers may not accurately reflect the stage of disease.

Metastatic carcinoma to the cervical nodes from an unknown head and neck primary site is a complex issue with no single definitive indication for neck dissection. Combined end points are acceptable, but age alone should not place patients in the high-risk category for carotid endarterectomy.

Dose reduction to one parotid gland can prevent xerostomia in many cases of advanced head and neck cancers, making it a viable option for minimizing radiation exposure.

β-catenin has been observed to be overexpressed in sebaceous cell carcinoma of the eyelid, suggesting a possible role in its pathogenesis. Further research is needed to explore its potential as a diagnostic biomarker.

Diffusion-weighted echo-planar MR imaging can differentiate pleomorphic adenoma and myoepithelial adenomas from other benign and malignant lesions, but diagnoses should be based on multiple criteria rather than ADC values alone.

The application of computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) in MR-mammography does not provide sufficient evidence to support whole lesion time curve distribution analysis as a critical factor in improving specificity.
